title: Triples, Cursors and Coverage
focus: The interview classic you must never fumble, an iterator over a tree, and greedy on a tree.

cards.title: 3Sum
patterns: Sort, then fix one and two-point the rest
Break early on a positive pivot
cards.trigger: Find triples, or k-tuples, summing to a target, with unique results required.
cards.recall: Write it from memory with both duplicate skips. Then answer: the outer skip uses `i > 0`, the inner skips run after a match. Say precisely why the two are different.
useWhen: 3Sum, 3Sum closest, 3Sum smaller
4Sum, and the general kSum recursion
Two sum on a sorted array
Any 'find unique tuples' question
Where a hash-set approach would produce duplicates you then have to clean up
template: if nums[i] > 0: break                       # sorted: no triple can sum to 0
if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]: continue   # skip duplicate pivots
while lo < hi and nums[lo] == nums[lo - 1]: lo += 1
while lo < hi and nums[hi] == nums[hi + 1]: hi -= 1
keyInsights: `i > 0` compares against the previous PIVOT you actually used. The inner skips run only after recording a match, comparing against the value just consumed
Sorting is not optional. It powers the two-pointer move, the duplicate skips and the early break all at once
The early break on a positive pivot is a real speedup on large inputs and costs one line
cards.trap: 'Now do 4Sum.' Two nested pivots plus the two-pointer, O(n^3), with duplicate skips at every level. If your 3Sum skips are hazy, 4Sum is unwriteable.

cards.title: BST Iterator
patterns: Pop, then push the right child's spine
cards.trigger: Iterate a BST in order, on demand, without flattening it first.
cards.recall: Write it from memory. Then answer the two claims in the complexity: why is space O(h) and not O(n), and why is `next` amortised O(1) despite the inner while loop?
useWhen: BST iterator, with next and hasNext
Kth smallest with repeated queries
Merge two BSTs in sorted order, run two iterators
Closest k values in a BST, two iterators moving outward
Any lazy in-order consumption
template: self._push_left(node.right)      # its right subtree's spine comes next
# Merging two BSTs in sorted order: two iterators, always advance the smaller.
# Same shape as merging two sorted lists.
keyInsights: The stack holds one node per level of the left spine, so it is bounded by the height, not the node count
Every node is pushed exactly once and popped exactly once across the whole iteration, so n calls do O(n) total work
This is the iterative inorder from Day 12, paused between pops. Recognising that means you already knew it
cards.trap: 'Support prev() as well.' A single stack cannot go backwards. You need parent pointers or a doubly threaded structure, and saying so is better than improvising.

cards.title: Greedy on a Tree
patterns: Decide at the parent, not the node
cards.trigger: Place the fewest items on a tree so that every node is covered by itself or a neighbour.
cards.recall: Name the three states a node can return before revealing. Then answer: why is the decision to place a camera made by the PARENT rather than by the node itself?
useWhen: Binary tree cameras, minimum nodes to cover a tree
Minimum vertex cover on a tree
Distribute coins in a binary tree
Any minimal-placement problem on a tree
Where a greedy leaf-upward argument beats a DP
template: # Three states returned from a subtree:
#   1 = this node is covered, but has no camera
if not node: return 1              # None counts as covered
if l == 0 or r == 0:               # a child is uncovered -> must place here
if l == 2 or r == 2:               # a child has a camera -> we are covered
return 0                           # both children merely covered -> we need it
return cameras + (1 if go(root) == 0 else 0)   # root may still be uncovered
keyInsights: Placing a camera at a leaf is always wasteful, since its parent covers strictly more. That is why cameras rise one level
The order of the three checks matters. Uncovered children must be handled before the covered case
The final root check is the only thing outside the recursion, and forgetting it undercounts by exactly one
cards.trap: 'Prove the greedy is optimal.' The exchange argument is: moving any leaf camera to its parent never covers less. Have it in one sentence.

cards.title: Counting Subsequences
cards.trigger: How many ways can one string appear as a subsequence of another.
cards.recall: State what `dp[i][j]` counts, then write both branches. Then answer: on a match, why do you ADD the two terms rather than take a max, and what does each term represent?
useWhen: Distinct subsequences
Count palindromic subsequences
Number of ways to form a target from sources
Any counting variant of a two-string DP
Where the optimisation version is LCS and the counting version is this
template: # dp[i][j] = number of ways s[:i] contains t[:j] as a subsequence
dp[i][0] = 1                       # one way to form the empty target
dp[i][j] += dp[i - 1][j - 1]   # OR use it to match t[j-1]
# Rolled to 1D: iterate j BACKWARDS so dp[j-1] is still the previous row
keyInsights: Counting means the two options are alternatives, so you add. Optimising means you pick one, so you max. That one word changes the operator
`dp[i][0] = 1` says there is exactly one way to match nothing, which is what makes the recursion bottom out correctly
The backwards inner loop in the 1D form is the same reason as 0/1 knapsack: keep the previous row's value available
cards.trap: 'The answer can be enormous.' In other languages you need 64-bit or a modulus. Mention it, because the problem statement usually guarantees it fits and interviewers probe whether you noticed.

cards.title: Shortest Path in a Grid
cards.trigger: Fewest steps through a grid where the move set is larger than four directions.
cards.recall: Write it from memory. Then answer the bug that costs people this problem: why must you mark a cell visited when you ENQUEUE it, not when you dequeue it?
useWhen: Shortest path in a binary matrix
Knight moves on a board
Minimum knight or king moves, any custom move set
Escape a maze in the fewest steps
Any unweighted shortest path over an implicit grid
template: q = deque([(0, 0, 1)])              # row, col, path length so far
if r == n - 1 and c == n - 1: return d
nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
if 0 <= nr < n and 0 <= nc < n and grid[nr][nc] == 0:
grid[nr][nc] = 1        # mark immediately, before it is processed
keyInsights: Marking on dequeue lets the same cell be enqueued many times before it is processed, which blows up the queue and can be exponential on dense grids
Carrying the distance in the tuple avoids a separate distance array and is the cleanest form for a single source
Eight directions instead of four changes nothing structurally, which is the point: the move set is data, not logic
cards.trap: 'Make it faster.' A-star with the Chebyshev distance heuristic is the intended answer. Name the heuristic; guessing at a heuristic that is not admissible is worse than not offering one.
